articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board will welcome three new members to its ranks. In voting yesterday, November 5, Michael Malione, Susy Struble, and Max Roman were elected to fill three vacancies on the school board e following Tuesday’s election. All three are parents of students in the district, and were running unopposed. They will join the board in December. Voters may have noticed one more candidate on the ballot for school board, Victoria Rosenbaum, She withdrew her intent to be a candidate but the ballots had already been printed. She publicly supported the other three candidates at the start of the race. “I’ve enjoyed the campaigning so far,” said Malione on election morning. “It’s been an unusual campaign because it hasn’t been contested, so I’ve had a chance to work with Max and Susy in advance of our officially starting.” The Alameda County Registrar of Voters began releasing results for the November 5 general election after the polls closed at 8:00 p.m. Tuesday night. The Post caught up with school board candidates Malione and Struble early on election day. “It’s been very exciting, it’s funny, because it’s not something I imagined ever doing years ago. But recently, after being involved in Piedmont by volunteering with the schools, it feels like the right step,” said Malione. “I feel the weight of it all. It was peculiar to see my name on the ballot, and I felt elegiac for the Republican party that I grew up with and the values I once believed my family shared,” said Susy Struble on Tuesday afternoon before picking up her kids. “Tonight, I’ll have a whiskey sour and will text furiously with friends,” she said with a smile. Current school board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen chose not to run for re-election for a second term, and Cory Smegal termed out after eight years of service on the board. The three board member elects will join Ruchi Medkehar and Lindsay Thomasson on the board.

Let us travel together By Pastor Jim Hopkins While we are not the first, last, or only to so, we do well to acknowledge that we live in tense and uncertain times. We live in times in which there is strong temptation to simply give up on ourselves and to give up on each other. The beautiful biblical story of Ruth gives us reason not to give in to the desperation or give up on each other. Scholars tell us that Ruth’s story was likely written down in a time when many in the lands of Israel and Judah believed that the problems they faced were the fault of outsiders in their country, foreigners in their land. They believe that Ruth’s story was told in order to counter the narratives of xenophobia (fear of the stranger) and replace them with a narrative of philoxenia (love of the stranger). The story begins with Naomi, an Israelite woman, who, during a famine moves to Moab with her husband and two sons. After the deaths of her husband and sons, Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem. She urges her Moabite daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, to stay in Moab. Orpah agrees to stay, but Ruth famously declares her loyalty to Naomi, saying, “Where you go, I will go; where you stay, I will stay.” I won’t go into the details of the story but in the end, Ruth the foreigner, blesses her new home her through her loyalty, her faith, her courage and ultimately, through a son, Obed, who becomes the grandfather of King David. The story ask the rhetorical question, “Where would we be without ‘outsiders’ like Ruth?” It urges its hearers not to disparage, disregard or disrespect foreigners in the land. It urges them not to give up on each other. The most poignant, and most well-known, scene, in the first chapter of Ruth is when Naomi informs Ruth and Orpah that she has decided to return to her home while urging them to stay in Moab. She says something to the effect of “There is nothing for me here and there is nothing for you there.” In Naomi’s words I hear the words of Mary Oliver in her poem “In Blackwater Woods.” To live in the world you must be able to do three things: to love what is mortal; to hold it against your bones knowing your own life See Religion Corner on page 28 JESSICA PAULY, Prospect Road My routine was messed up this weekend anyway because I was on a 6-1/2 hour flight back from New York. articles.text: Text reprinted from Treasure Island Museum News In 1944, the US Navy charged 50 Black sailors with mutiny for refusing to load munitions following an explosion at Port Chicago, near Concord, which killed 320 people, mostly Black enlisted men. The Port Chicago 50 were wrongly convicted and only recently exonerated. Treasure Island Museum partnered with the Treasure Island Development Group, Port Chicago Naval Magazine National Memorial, East Bay Regional Park District, Treasure Island Development Authority, and Hood Design Studio to create the only permanent monument honoring the Port Chicago 50 that is fully accessible to the public. It was dedicated and unveiled in Panorama Park on Yerba Buena Island on October 24 this year. The unveiling was featured on two local newscasts: The local CBS affiliate’s coverage includes contemporaneous photographs and details about the explosion and trial. The NBC station’s coverage features an interview with TIM Vice President Walt Bilofsky and considers the significance of the exoneration of the Port Chicago 50. Photos courtesy of Cross Media International A permanent monument honoring the Port Chicago 50 was dedicated in Panorama Park on Yerba Buena Island on October 24, 2024. Members of the press, local leaders, and island neighbors filled Panorama Park for the dedication ceremony. It became a celebration of progress and community. articles.text: In support of existing businesses Editor: In last week’s edition of the Post, a City Council Candidate suggested possible support for “a funky clothing shop” as a new type of business for our limited city space. I’m writing to remind residents that we have had the benefit of a non-profit, resale shop, Dress Best For Less, on Piedmont Avenue, for over 40 years. It is considered one of the largest single donors to Piedmont Schools and beyond, donating approximately $1.2 million since its founding in 1982. I’ve found some funky Halloween items there over the years. articles.text: The National Weather Service has issued a Red Flag Warning that includes Piedmont; it began at 11 a.m. on Tuesday, November 5. The Piedmont Fire Department has received a “spot forecast” confirming heightened fire risk locally during this period due to strong offshore winds and dry conditions. As of press time the warning is scheduled to last until Thursday, November 7, at 7:00 a.m. The last red flag warning was October 16, and two days later the Keller Fire burned parts of the Oakland Hills. PG&E has issued plans for rolling blackouts in parts of the Bay Area. Based on Tuesday’s conditions, approximately PG&E 22,000 customers fall within the scope for a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS), but none within Piedmont. Check this map for the status of power outages which could begin Wednesday at 12:01 a.m. Pgealerts.alerts.pge.com/outage-tools/outage-map/ The City of Piedmont reminds residents that fires which start during red flag conditions can spread quickly and unpredictably. According to City Communication Manager Echa Schneider Red flag warnings are rare for the city, and prior to these last two, no Red Flag warnings had been issued to the city since 2022. “Use extreme caution when operating BBQs, power equipment, or other heat sources, such as idling cars,” urges the City. “Park offstreet to keep streets clear for emergency vehicles. Call 9-1-1 immediately if you see signs of fire.” The Fire Department has increased staffing for the event and will be patrolling the city during the period of highest fire risk. Residents should follow the progress of the weather and take steps now, to be ready to evacuate if needed. Preparations • Sign up for AC Alert emergency notifications. In an emergency, the City will use AC Alert to send instructions about protective actions. for AC Alert emergency notifications https://member.everbridge. net/453003085612570/new • Keep your phone on and with you to receive alerts, even while sleeping. Do not use “do not disturb” mode during high-risk weather. • Pack or refresh your go-bag and place it by your front door. • Review evacuation routes. Identify two paths out of your neighborhood by car and two by foot. • Back your car into your garage or driveway, so you are able to leave quickly. For more information on how to prepare for wildfire evacuation, see piedmont.ca.gov/wildfire. Any updates will be posted at piedmont.ca.gov/RedFlag Potential areas near Piedmont may experience a planned PG&E power shutoff beginning Wednesday 12-2 a.m. Around 22,000 Alameda County households may be affected.

articles.text: Founder Dr. Kathy Hull honored in special tribute George Mark Children’s House marked a milestone with its 20th Anniversary Gala at the iconic Fairmont Hotel in San Francisco on Friday, October 25. This special evening brought together more than 500 donors, families, staff, and board members to celebrate two decades of unwavering commitment to providing exceptional care to seriously ill children and their families. The event featured speeches from founder Dr. Kathy Hull, CEO Shekinah Eliassen, and award-winning author Amie Lands. Adding a personal touch to the evening was former George Mark patient Charlie Cleberg, who shared his experiences and the profound impact the organization had on his life, alongside his parents Kathy and Joe. The gala was emceed by Betty Yu of KTVU, infusing the event with warmth and elegance. “Tonight, we honor not just the past 20 years of compassionate care, but also the countless lives touched by the services provided at George Mark. Our mission remains as vital today as it was when we began,” said Dr. Kathy Hull. The gala underscored the organization’s legacy of supporting families during challenging times. Ann Kennedy, Leslie Bond, Joan Cox, Janie Edwards, Maureen Sansevero Dr. Kathy Hull Shekinah Eliassen & Kathy Hull DJ Grubb, Toby Taylor, Audrey Grubb, Diane Taylor Betty Yu KTVU Report, Gala Emcee Kristin Hull & Jordan Cortez Cathy Glazier, Liz Tuan, Sarah Abel, Julie Veveiros, Terry Patton Anthony Riggins, Dr. Kathy Hull, Lee Hamrick “This celebration is a testament to the extraordinary generosity of our community. Each contribution helps us continue our critical work, ensuring that every child and family receives the care they deserve without ever seeing a bill,” added George Mark House CEO Shekinah Eliassen. Fundraising efforts during the gala were met with generosity – and proceeds contributing to the sustainability and expansion of George Mark Children’s House’s services. The evening epitomized the spirit of community and the shared commitment to making a difference in the lives of children and families. “In the face of adversity, George Mark Children’s House stands as a beacon of hope and support,” said Andrew Pitcairn, a father whose daughter experienced the compassionate care at George Mark House. “The stories shared tonight highlight the resilience and courage of the families they serve, and it’s an honor to be part of this incredible community,” he added. San Francisco’s Chief of Protocol, Maryam Muduroglu, honored Dr. Kathy Hull and George Mark with a City of San Francisco Proclamation. In addition, a Congressional Commendation in honor of George Mark and Dr. Kathy Hull from U.S. Representative Eric Swalwell, whose district includes San Leandro, was read by Betty Yu, with the Commendation inserted into the official Congressional Record. These recognitions highlight the significance of their work within the community.

articles.text: Children are natural born scientists – curious about the world and picking up new information every single day. One easy and useful way to learn is to ask an expert! We’ve gathered a small handful of questions from kids who were curious about animals, nature, and the Zoo, answered by our Learning and Engagement staff. What is your favorite animal to study? Every Zoo expert will have a different answer for this. But for me, I adore the clever animals that are amazing problem solvers - species like orangutans, ravens, and octopuses. They really make me appreciate how incredible animals can be, and it helps me respect wildlife even more. There must be so much more to discover about animals that we still don’t even know about. What inspired you to become a scientist? I have been obsessed with animals since I was a little kid. Whenever my family would visit a new city, I would beg to go visit the zoo there. There were tons of different species from all over the world, and they were all so unique and cool in their way. I read every single animal book they had at the library so that I could pick up all the coolest animal facts. Best of all, I took time to look for animals whenever I was visiting a park, in a garden, or visiting a beach. Nature was all around me, and that was plenty of inspiration all on its own. What will the rainforest be like in 100 years? It’s tough to know for sure, but many human actions are harming the rainforest. Scientists understand these issues and have solutions. I believe that a century from now, rainforests can thrive Patrick Wolff talks to Zoo guests about Xosha the hedgehog. again. You can help by composting, walking or biking, and reusing items. articles.text: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time for their Fall play. The play will come to life in three showings Thursday to Saturday, November 14-16, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Fifteen-year-old Christopher Boone lives in Swindon, a quiet working-class town on the outskirts of London with his single father. After Christopher’s neatly structured world is sent unraveling by the death of his neighbor’s beloved dog, he embarks on the adventure of a lifetime. This powerful drama weaves together the excitement of mystery and adventure as well as heartwarming and heartbreaking aspects of love, trust, and family as Christopher’s investigation alters the course of his life. This production of The Curious Incident is Simon Stephen’s abridged theatrical adaptation of Mark Haddon’s 2003 best-selling novel, which was translated into 44 languages and sold more than 5.5 million copies worldwide. The first production in 2012 in London’s West End, won seven Olivier awards including Best Play. On Broadway in New York it won the 2015 Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Play, and five Tony Awards, including one for Best Play. This abridged, 90-minute version has been performed by more than 60 schools in the UK. articles.text: Four years ago, on September 29, 2021, an emergency meeting was called by Piedmont’s first year football coach. The Piedmont High Varsity football team faced a crisis. After suffering their fourth consecutive defeat, with a staggering combined score of 165-60, the program was in disarray. The situation worsened when one of the five senior players was sidelined for at least three games due to injury, leaving the roster with just 17 players, including eight sophomores. The numbers simply did not add up, and the varsity season was abruptly canceled. The cancellation was a devastating blow, particularly for the healthy seniors who had hoped to finish their high school careers on the field. The community, steeped in over a century of football tradition, was left grappling with questions. Was this the end of football at Piedmont High? Fear, uncertainty, and doubt loomed large. Yet, on that fateful evening of September 29th, a group of determined parents and student-athletes gathered in the bleachers at Witter Field. Among them were the resilient sophomores of the Class of 2025. Eighteen strong, they undertook a mission to restore Piedmont football to its historic glory and re-establish Friday Night Lights as the showcase of PHS school spirit. Despite being predicted to finish 1-9 the following year in 2023, the team defied all expectations. They emerged as league champions, achieving the remarkable feat while playing all their games on the road due to Witter Field’s reconstruction. This season, the team faced a new challenge, moving up to a more competitive division due its stellar performance last year. And now, once again, they remain undefeated in league play. The Class of 2025 has proven to be extraordinary. Their legacy is one of resilience and triumph over adversity. These 17 year olds may not fully grasp the magnitude of their achievements, but their efforts have laid a foundation for the program’s ongoing success. Their story is one of inspiration, not just for the football team but for the entire community. The team has one more home game this regular season – Friday, November 8th, 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field. This is the last chance to witness this special group in action. Beyond their incredible journey over the past three years, this team possesses exceptional heart and talent. Their legacy will ensure continued success for the program, but the magic they bring to the field is something you do not want to miss. Do yourself a favor and come watch the show – one last time. Highlander Nation... Let’s Ride.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team showed promise of a bright future this year. A 6-5 victory over Encinal on Friday, November 1, and an 11-9 win against Lick-Wilmerding in the first round of the league playoff consolation bracket and marked the team’s most wins in seven years. Piedmont concluded its season with a 10-12 record. The win against Encinal gave the Highlanders fifth place in the final of the Western Alameda County Conference Tournament. “It was a fun game. I think that we were in the right mindset and they really wanted it. We came ready and it was an aggressive game. I didn’t know this result matched 2017 and I’m really happy to hear that. It makes me proud to work with this program,” said coach Georgia Lewis. The team hasn’t had a winning season since 2014 when former head coach and current assistant coach Sarah Mooney led the school to a 16-6 record. “It’s really an honor. I don’t think any of us could imagine that outcome at the start of the season, I’m so proud of how hard we worked throughout the season. To do it without a home pool means a lot,” junior Viviane Burke said. “I’m so proud of how we worked and how far we’ve come,” added junior Abigail Jacoby, the team’s leading scorer. Piedmont’s win over Encinal required a stout defense. The Highlanders trailed 2-0 early and 4-3 in the third quarter. Young scored the game-winning goal with 5:23 left and the rest was left up to the defense. “I knew we had one mission and that was to protect the ball. I kept repeating how much time we had left and just tried to push people to the end. I’m really happy and proud of us,” Burke said. “I thought we were down and I was yelling at people. But once it was over, that was the most amazing surprise,” Jacoby added. Looking ahead to 2025, Piedmont could be on track for its first post-season North Coast Section playoff berth since 2016. This year’s team will graduate just three players and likely will bring back seven juniors, two sophomores, and one freshman, including key starters Jacoby, Burke, Rachel Young, Sydney Olson and Esme Krumins. “I’m really excited for next year just to see if we can keep building what we have,” coach Lewis said. 6-5 win over Encinal In the first quarter, Encinal got out to a 2-0 lead by the 4:10 mark. Piedmont missed the mark on four shot attempts before getting on the board with 35 seconds left when Jacoby sent in PHS’ first goal. Both teams traded possession in the second quarter with Piedmont finding several near chances, including Krumins hitting a shot off the crossbar in the early minutes. Jacoby then tied the game with 2:45 left, then took the lead on a 6-on-5 opportunity when Olson assisted Young for a goal with 1:59 left. However, Encinal scored two straight goals to take a 4-3 lead with 22 seconds left. It was more of the same backand-forth possessions in the third quarter with both teams having good chances. Burke had a shot saved in the first minute, while goalie Chloe Graham had a big save in close distance around two minutes into the quarter. Jacoby then tied the game at 4-4 with 3:28 to go, but Encinal retook the lead on its next possession. As the quarter wound down, Jacoby had a shot tipped onto the crossbar with 50 seconds left, but PHS retained possession. Olson then sent a pass to Burke for the goal with 38 seconds left, 5-5. articles.text: Giacomo Puccini’s opera La Bohème will be performed at Opera San José November 16 through December 1. Snow will fall in San José on Saturday, November 16 when one of opera’s greatest love stories, Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème, returns to Opera San José in a production set in Paris at Christmastime, following the aftermath of World War I. Set in bustling Parisian cafés, raucous parties and chilly garrets, this opera follows a pair of doomed lovers and their coterie of artist friends chasing happiness against impossible odds. Opera San José Artist-in-Residence tenor Wooyoung Yoon stars as the poet Rodolfo, with sopranos Kearstin Piper Brown and Mikayla Sager alternating as Mimì, in this tantalizing tale of young artists living on the edge. “With a backdrop of Christmastime in Paris, this production of La Bohème will usher audiences well into the holidays,” said Opera San José General Director and CEO Shawna Lucey. “Puccini’s brilliant score and heart-rending arias bring to life one of opera’s most exquisite works, making it both a great favorite of longtime operagoers and a perfect introduction for those new to this art form.” Written by Puccini; featuring a libretto by Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa; and based on Henri Murger’s episodic novel “Scènes de la vie de bohème” (“Scenes of Bohemian Life”), “La Bohème” premiered in 1896 at Teatro Regio in Turin, Italy. The opera features three backto-back showstoppers in Act I alone: Rodolfo’s famous aria “Che gelida manina,” followed by Mimì’s “Mi chiamano Mimì” and the couple’s duet “O soave fanciulla.” Puccini’s own life as a student in Milan influenced many aspects of the opera. Audiences will experience this production in the beautifully gilded historic California Theatre, one of the world’s most elegant and intimate opera houses. Opera San José Resident Stage Director Michelle Ainna Cuizon will make her mainstage directorial debut, while Opera San José Music Director Joseph Marcheso will conduct this masterpiece, performed in Italian with English and Spanish supertitles. Tenor Wooyoung Yoon’s recent roles include lead performances in The Magic Flute, Rigoletto, and Romeo and Juliet for Opera San José, and the title role in La Damnation de Faust with the Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional de Costa Rica. Yoon also premiered a concert commemorating the heroism of Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara which debuted at Carnegie Hall. He returned to Carnegie Hall this past spring as a soloist in Hagenberg’s Illuminare and in Misa Criolla. To purchase tickets ($58– $215) for the performance at California Theatre (345 S. 1st St., San Jose), visit operasj.org or call 408-437-4450.

articles.text: The internationally renowned opera Everest, composed by Joby Talbot with libretto by Gene Scheer, will come to the California Academy of Sciences in a bold, immersive new film iteration. It will be shown from this Friday, November 8 through November 17. Based on the true story of an ill-fated 1996 expedition to summit Mount Everest, this evocative production scales a breathtaking final climb to the top of the world’s highest mountain using intricate graphic imagery and a soaring sound world. The work will have audiences climb to new heights in the immersive environment of the Morrison Planetarium, one of the largest and most advanced all-digital domes in the world. Everest, which won the International Opera award in London as best world premiere in 2015. follows three real climbers: Rob Hall, Doug Hansen, and Beck Weathers. The experience begins with Rob, the expedition leader, who has just reached the summit 30 minutes past the safe turnaround time. His client, Doug, is 40 feet below him. In a separate timeline we meet Beck, dreaming on a lower part of the mountain about his life back in Texas, and particularly about his daughter, Meg. Doug finally reaches the summit but is struggling to maintain consciousness. It’s up to Rob to get him safely back down the mountain. Meanwhile, a large storm hits below the summit, making their descent even more treacherous. Through Rob’s memories and an extraordinary phone call, audiences also meet Rob’s pregnant wife, Jan, in New Zealand. As the climbers struggle to reach safety through the storm, we experience with them the brutal realities of Everest and the power of human conviction. As the men push the physical limits of human ability, the crackling mountain, the prevailing wind, the power of nature abounds. The immersive work moves between the climbers realities on the mountain, and that of their loved ones far below. With a soaring and impassioned score, “Everest: Opera in the Planetarium” will be presented in the groundbreaking medium of a powerful opera which is transformed into a riveting graphic novel film projected across the arched dome of the planetarium. The event, produced by San Francisco contemporary opera nonprofit Opera Parallèle, will feature a rich recording of the renowned opera cast and orchestra led by Maestro Nicole Paiement. Meanwhile, the animations will come to life through facial tracking technology which will transform the impassioned singer’s facial movements during the time of recording into animated graphics which follow the singer’s voice. The result is an immersive, truly unique operatic experience which is further enriched by the planetarium’s state-of-theart surround sound. From the moment that viewers enter the venue, they will be transported into a stylized, animated mountainscape. With a directional surround-soundscape, they will feel every crack of ice, the menacing storms and the powerful voices of the cast. Tickets ($50 general, $30 student, $100 Pay It Forward) for the show at Morrison Planetarium (55 Music Concourse Dr., San Francisco) are available at operaparallele.org/everest. articles.text: Film explores deep sea mining Beta Space: Patty Chang and David Kelley is now on view at the San José Museum of Art through June 1, 2025. Taking the form of an open laboratory, the visual artists’ newest multimedia installation features their first inquiry into a site without human inhabitants: the deep sea. Organized by museum assistant curator Juan Omar Rodriguez, the exhibition explores the animal and mineral history of the deep sea. “Taking a poetic approach to the loops that bind our lives with the deep sea, Chang and Kelley invite us to think critically about our responsibilities to other forms of life as we navigate multiple climate crises,” said Rodriguez. The Los Angeles-based artists will premiere the first iteration of their newest multidisciplinary project, Hydrophobia (2024). This work revolves around the question of how to imagine a human relationship to nature’s ocean floor in the context of technology, law, electrification and cycles of global resource extraction. This inquiry was inspired by the increasing demands for electric cars, particularly in California. While pressures rise to pivot away from fossil fuels as terrestrial mining becomes more difficult, automakers and other parties are increasingly interested in extracting minerals needed for making and maintaining electric vehicles from ever-more remote sites, such as the ocean floor. With this growing interest in deep-sea mining, the International Seabed Authority (ISA) is currently working to draft regulations to permit deep sea mining within the next few years. In Hydrophobia Chang and Kelley situate the recent activities of the ISA within increasing scales of time — the immediate climate crisis; the thirty year context of mining behind the ISA’s legislative efforts; 150 years of modern oceanography, beginning with the 1872 global expedition of the HMS Challenger; and the millions of years it took for organic matter, such as shark teeth, to become the potato-sized nodules of rare minerals coveted by mining companies and automakers today. The presentation of Hydrophobia at SJMA features a new film consisting of footage of the ISA’s convenings in Kingston, Jamaica; visits to HMS Challenger museum collections throughout England; and a 3-D animation of the deep sea. Housed within a large wooden structure with kinetic elements alongside by glass and ceramic sculptures featuring deep sea specimens, this multimedia installation will model an open laboratory that weaves all these various threads of research and time together. The San José Museum of Art (110 South Market Street, San Jose) is open 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Thursdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Fridays and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will present the global debut of the painter Amy Sherald’s first mid-career survey on Saturday, November 16. The largest and most comprehensive presentation of Sherald’s work to date, “American Sublime” will bring together nearly 50 paintings made from 2007 to the present, from her poetic early portraits to the incisive, moving figure paintings for which she is best known. Iconic portraits of Michelle Obama and Breonna Taylor will be joined by early works never or rarely seen by the public. Also included will be new works created specifically for the exhibition, such as the artist’s first triptych, “Ecclesia (The Meeting of Inheritance and Horizons),” on view for the first time. A centerpiece of the show will be “For Love, and for Country,” a work which references Alfred Eisenstaedt’s photograph of a sailor kissing a woman in Times Square in 1945, just as World War II ended. Sherald’s 10-foot tall work envisions the embrace happening between two men in a rebuttal of the rising discrimination and restrictive legislation against the LGBTQ+ community at that time. Another evocative work by Sherald, “If You Surrendered to the Air, You Could Ride It,” alludes to “Lunch atop a Skyscraper,” Charles C. Ebbets’s famous photograph of steel workers taking a break on a construction site high above Manhattan. Sherald’s work points to the greatness of American industry, and the Black workers whose contributions to these advancements were largely disregarded from history. The exhibition will consider the impact of Sherald’s work on contemporary art and on American culture, as she addresses historical omissions of Black figures from the history of figure painting. She has described her paintings as offering a resting place – an opportunity to see Black figures not in contention, racialized or politicized, but simply being. The resulting body of work is a deeply resonant ode to everyday people and a convincing tes- “First Lady Michelle Obama,” Amy Sherald, 2018. SFMOMA will present the global debut of the painter Amy Sherald from this Saturday, November 16 through March 9, 2025. tament that, as Sherald has said, images can change the world. “Amy Sherald is one of the most important portraitists working today, and we are honored to present her first mid-career survey at SFMOMA,” said Christopher Bedford, a Director of SFMOMA. “Her unique and exquisite renderings of her subjects encourage close looking, curiosity and awe.” “By creating images of Black men, women and children at ease, with few markers of place, time or context beyond the clothes they wear, Sherald has invented an entirely new form of contemporary figurative painting. Her approach goes beyond portraiture to enact new conditions for seeing, feeling and understanding shared humanity,” said curator Sarah Roberts. “In the spirit of great American artists like Edward Hopper, Alice Neel and Kerry James Marshall, Sherald’s works reframe our understanding of American culture. Her paintings invite viewers to recognize and move beyond preconceived ideas and engage in more expansive thinking about race, representation and the wide-open possibilities and complexities of every individual,” she added. SFMOMA, located at 151 Third Street in San Francisco, is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, and 12 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $23 student, free 18 and younger) are available at sfmoma.org/visit.

Throughout my life I have always been impressed by people who could quote poetry and people who could draw. There are so many ways to draw inspiration. Humanity must always be on the alert. That’s the way it was this past weekend. On Friday evening, there was a rehearsal of the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra in First Church Berkeley. A scheduling conflict prevented me from attending their concert on Saturday night, but attending the rehearsal gave me the opportunity to see their longstanding conductor David Ramadanoff in action. YPSO is one of the oldest youth orchestras in the world, and Ramadanoff has led them for 36 years. When you are a conductor, you need to think of many things. The first thing that is apparent is that Ramadanoff knows how to be encouraging. This is the inspiration kids need and they rise to the occasion. During the rehearsal I admired the full tone of the orchestra. Their ensemble was always attentive, both to the music and the conductor. One of the things that is always a pleasure for me to see is the enthusiasm exhibited by young musicians. The YPSO has tons of it. They also play with discipline. When you add all of these things together, the result is inspiring music making. articles.text: The Art of the Stroll: celebrating leisurely journeys Michael Stehr returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts with his most recent exhibition, The Art of the Stroll. With this group of 30 new paintings, Stehr explores the activity of strolling as a source of outstanding inspiration. Stehr’s work demonstrates that while moving slowly and deliberately through our environments, the stroll can be much more than a way of getting from one location to another. The stroll can be used as a means of accessing the wide range of beauty that always surrounds us. In this group of 30 new paintings, Stehr celebrates inspiration from a variety of locations, including France, Italy, Lake Tahoe, Greece, the East Coast, Napa, and the California foothills. Compositions include both man-made beauty, such as the architecture that lines the River Seine in Paris, along with the boundless array of beauty supplied by Mother Nature, as seen in landscapes from Giverny, Kefalonia, and the Stanislaus River. Stehr’s exhibit will open with a reception on November 15, at 6 p.m. in the Center for the Arts. He will offer remarks to provide context for the exhibit. To attend the reception please RSVP to mstehrart@gmail.com. The 80 paintings that will be on display may be viewed during gallery hours on the weekends of November 16-17, 23-24, and 30-31 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Photo of the artist at work ®

The program will feature a variety of surprising, engaging pieces including music by Sergei Prokofiev, George Gershwin, Jean Sibelius, Giuseppe Martucci, Luca Ballerini and three original pieces by Bocus. Bocus, who will conduct and lead the group, said, “Music often thrives on the unexpected, whether through the intentional use of sharps and flats or the surprising moments of inspiration that arise during its creation. This season, we’ve put together a program that celebrates both the notes on the score and the serendipitous elements that shape the best music.” The music of Duke Ellington Head back to PCA this Sunday for a jazz-filled late afternoon concert beginning at 4:30 Classically trained mandolinist Achille Bocus, with a small ensemble of leading Bay Area musicians will perform an afternoon concert at PCA this Saturday. p.m., when In the Tradition piano trio of Bill Jackman, Michael Jones and Albert Brooks will play a tribute to jazz composer, bandleader and pianist Duke Ellington. Jackman, playing with the trio for the past 30 years, was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher, who for several decades presided over the grand piano at the former Solomon Grundy’s restaurant (now Skates) on the Berkeley Marina. Jackman is also a Lupita Records musician Catch the piano trio In the Tradition at PCA this Sunday afternoon, as they play a tribute to jazz composer, bandleader and pianist Duke Ellington. who has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader who has played throughout the Bay Area for over 30 years. After studying music at the University of Northern Colorado, he moved to the Bay Area in the mid-1970s, where he played with many icons including Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders and Buddy Montgomery. As a sideman and bandleader, Jones has served as the music director for the Golden Gate Library Summer Concert and Jam Session series in Oakland for 23 years. Albert Brooks, a retired physician, grew up dancing to Latin music in the South Bronx and playing these rhythms on any percussion instrument he could get his hands on. Along with Latin drumming, he added trap drums to his musical offerings. He has juggled his growth as a drummer with the demands of being an obstetrician-gynecologist in the East Bay for three decades after graduating from the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University in New York City. articles.text: The Marsh in Berkeley presents the premiere of Stephanie Weisman’s 180 Days. To Die. To Live., from this Friday, November 8 through November 24. A compelling and deeply personal look at those facing imminent death and the living who help them navigate final choices, the work features actors Anne Darragh and Josiah Polhemus; playwright and founder of The Marsh, Stephanie Weisman; and acclaimed TheatreWorks Founder and Artistic Director Emeritus, Robert Kelley, to direct. Seen through two people’s end-of-life journeys, the play finds a woman coping with the final precious months of her husband’s life, and those of a friend’s, as they are both diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. While the husband undergoes chemotherapy, the friend opts for no treatment – with both finally deciding to use California’s assisted physician medical-aid in dying, legalized in 2016 but still largely unknown. While reliving the overwhelming and yet universal experience of saying goodbye to loved ones, the play also offers humorous looks at the bureaucratically convoluted eligibility requirements and the challenges of navigating the healthcare system in general. As the woman – a widow and cancer survivor herself – learns the ins and outs of how life may end in a hospital setting, she takes up qigong and other alternative healing practices to stay vital as she moves through caretaking, grief and bereavement. 180 Days. To Die. To Live. offers audiences a firsthand look at the tough choices and endless love available at the end-of-life, touching on personal decisions, healthcare options and legal considerations. Tickets ($20-$35 sliding scale, $50 and $100 reserved) and showtimes for performances at The Marsh Berkeley (2120 Allston Way) are available at themarsh.org. Anne Daragh, Stephanie Weisman and Josiah Polhemus are featured in The Marsh’s premiere of 180 Days. To Die. To Live., from November 8 through November 24.

articles.text: The Art of Racing in the Rain is an engaging and moving story with an insightful voice-over delivered by a golden retriever, Enzo (Kevin Costner). I know… but it’s perfect. His owner is Denny Swift (Milo Ventimiglia), a race car driver/ instructor who is known for his remarkable ability to navigate his race car at high speeds around tight Of course, this art is not just an extraordinary ability to race in the rain, but is a metaphor for negotiating life through difficult circumstances, unexpected curves and profound sadness. Enzo is devoted to Denny and when Denny falls in love with the charming and kind Eve (Amanda Seyfield) – though it takes him a while to warm up to her – he eventually accepts her as part of Soon Denny and Eve have a child, Zoe (Rya Kiera)), who over the years grows into a sweet 7-year-old adored by Enzo. But it’s at this point that a shadow falls over the family. Eve becomes seriously ill. At first she simply doesn’t feel like herself, but then, after passing out on a run through the woods, she is diagnosed with brain cancer. Soon, the inevitable outcome becomes clear and while Denny sits by her side and struggles to cope with her illness, it is Enzo who remains by her side While Eve receives treatment, she stays with her affluent parents, Trish and Maxwell (Kathy Milo Ventimiglia and Butler in The Art of Racing in the Rain Bates and Martin Donovan) along with Zoe, while Denny, having stopped racing, works in a garage in order to be near her. He also declines an offer by Ferrari to test their new prototype cars, explaining he has to be near Eve. Of course there is unexpected drama when the grandparents sue Denny for custody of Zoe, arguing that Denny will be too involved with his racing career to properly take care of their daughter. And so the story takes a dramatic turn that involves a court hearing that could result in Denny losing access to Zoe. With the unexpected encouragement of Enzo, Denny risks everything as a parent, insisting that despite his career, he should have full custody of Zoe. Throughout the trial Enzo watches and comments, wishing he was a human, and believing that one day he will be. The Art of Racing in the Rain is a family-friendly film in all respects, and will be enjoyed by youngsters as well as tweens, teens, and adults. The best part of the story is the raspy voice of Enzo, delivered perfectly by Kevin Costner. The Art of Racing in the Rain. Directed by Simon Curtis. articles.text: The Rocketeer, based on the graphic novel written by Dave Stevens, should appeal to a whole new generation of kids. Sure, it’s retro, set in 1942, and carried with it the hope that it would be the beginning of a superhero franchise. Alas, for reasons that remain inexplicable, it failed to find an audience, and never caught the imagination of those kids for which it was intended. Hence, no Rocketeer II. But after a quarter century since its release and after a bevy of superhero movies, its special effects and energetic story can seem fresh and compelling, even with the absence of CGI. Set in Los Angeles, the year is 1938. The film opens with Cliff Secord (Billy Campbell), a test pilot and barnstormer, who finds in his crashed bi-plane a strange looking dual rocket pack with a leather harness. He takes it to his favorite mechanic, Peevy Peabody (Alan Arkin), to ask what he can make of it. It’s only later that Cliff comes to realize that the pack was stolen from Howard Hughes (Terry O’ Quinn) by a gang of thieves (who had hidden the pack in Billy’s plane. They are led by one gangster-type named Eddie Valentine (Paul Sorvino). Predictably, not only does the U.S. government want the package, but it’s also being sought after by a cohort of nefarious Nazis who immediately see the potential in creating an army of rocket men using the package as a weapon to take over the U.S. Of course, Cliff and Peevy figure out how to tweak the rockets and Cliff soon finds himself going vertical into the sky. It’s a rush. And thus is born what became known as the Rocketeer. A sceen from The Rocketeer

articles.text: A large group showed up last week for Walking on Wednesdays. Among those participating were Gloria DaSilva with K-9 best friend Lola, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Brenda Ferrero, Adrienne Hamlin, Claudine Bach, Margaret Leunig, Sheila Leunig, Helen Dong, Sharona Fischrup, Kathy Rolfson, Dave DeRoche, Sherry Jacobs, Peter Munoz, Lois Price, Marj Blackwell, Jill Day, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Irene Thompson, Ron Day, Joanne Larson, Bonnie Sherwood, Jim Kellogg, Melba Yee, Sandra Cook, Quincy Dong, Martin Levy, Bob Wong, Peggy Shultz, Denny McGee, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Judy Love, Lisa Euphrat, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Phil Witte, Joyce Ahern, Priscilla Wanerus, Bill Ahern, Leigh Sorensen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Stella Houston’s goddaughter Leilani Ching, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Melissa Clark, and Kim Blumberg who were walking with them for the first time. Last Wednesday, October 30, the Walking on Wednesdays group had its annual pre-Halloween tour of Mountain View Cemetery. They are pictured in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum. Forty-six walkers with four K-9 best friends were on hand. The tour was conducted by longtime docent Jane Leroe. Jane has an extensive knowledge of the Mountain View Cemetery and loves sharing it. Jane’s women’s tour of the historic cemetery included some famous women who made significant contributions in law, medicine, education, and architecture. The suffragist movement which resulted in women gaining the right to vote in California in 1911 was also part of it. Jane took the group inside to the mausoleum’s chapel for her introductory remarks. Seeing it was a treat. It was serene with lots of marble. In the early 1860s a group of twelve leading businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and the 13th mayor of Oakland (1867 to 1869), decided the area needed a private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better. They bought 200 acres of fields far from the center of Oakland at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery was established in 1863. Twenty-six acres were added later. Approximately 170,000 people are buried at Mountain View, and there is room for an additional equal number. The founders’ contract with Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park and Stanford University, called for him to get $1,000. No women were involved in the cemetery’s development. Some made good use of their deceased husbands’ money when they took up permanent residence at Mountain View. There are also many self-made, successful women buried in the cemetery. Jane led the group through the back of the mausoleum and up a hill to the Colton tomb. David Colton was the business manager for the “Big 4,” the men who built the transcontinental railroad. These men should probably be called the “Big 4½.” After David’s death Ellen was involved in a lawsuit in which she showed the men’s correspondence telling how they bribed lawmakers. Then it was over to the grave of Clara Bedell, a well-known madame in San Francisco in the latter part of the 19th century. Her “house of ill-repute” was located on Post Street near Union Square in San Francisco. In 1891, at the age of 37, she was found dead in her room. It appeared she had mixed opium with some wine and overdosed. Three years after her death she was named the beneficiary of a $10,000 life insurance policy of a local judge. Jane noted many women with remarkable histories and accomplishments. Miranda Lux provided $500,000 for California schools. Chloe Buckel was orphaned at age four but became a doctor and an advocate for education. Mary McHenry Keith was the first woman to graduate from Hastings Law School. Ina Donna Coolbrith was California’s first poet laureate. German-born Emma Marwedel started the first free kindergarten on the West Coast. Sara Lemmon is responsible for the California Poppy being named the State flower. Mary Williams was the New York World’s only women cartoonist and advocated for women’s suffrage in her work. Kate Kirkham provided free medical services for the poor and created a Fabiola Society Hospital that was bought by Kaiser. Anna Head started the K-12 school in 1887 that still bears her name today. Architect Julia Morgan, likely the most famous woman buried at Mountain View, is in a family plot. She is listed sixth on a plaque with other family members because she wanted to be buried with them, and let her monuments reflect her accomplishments. Jane told these stories and more in a fact-filled, highly enjoyable tour on a lovely day. At the morning’s end the walkers expressed thanks to Jane for a most enjoyable pre-Halloween tour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: One of the keen pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a discussion of it afterward. This month’s film is Bread and Tulips (Pane e Tulipani in its original language), which was advertised at the time of its release in 2000 as “the best Italian comedy of the year.” Some decided, after seeing it, that it’s the best comedy of 2000, period. There’s no doubt, however, that its Italian setting gives it a special quality, especially since that setting is Venice in all its labyrinthine charm. The Italian temperament enhances the tale, too, with its broad gestures, uninhibited expression, and quick-toignite passions. It all begins when Rosalba Barletta (Licia Maglietta), a Neapolitan-born housewife, finds herself stranded during a family vacation. Instead of waiting for her controlling and unfaithful husband to retrieve her, she decides to hitchhike her way home, and then – ah! – impulsively detours to Venice. That’s when things get even more wacky and romantic. A waiter, played by Bruno Ganz, starts to make Rosalba’s heartbeat to quicken. In the meantime her husband has sent a bumbling detective to search her out. After showing up in Venice himself, the hubby gets the hots for a holistic masseuse. Funny compilations ensue. Bread and Tulips will be screened on Thursday, November 14, at 1:00 p.m. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the event takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration may be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the series is the classic romantic comedy Roman Holiday, the movie that introduced Audrey Hepburn to the world, and co-starring Gregory Peck., It will be shown on December 12th. A large group showed up last week for Walking on Wednesdays. Among those participating were Gloria DaSilva with K-9 best friend Lola, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Brenda Ferrero, Adrienne Hamlin, Claudine Bach, Margaret Leunig, Sheila Leunig, Helen Dong, Sharona Fischrup, Kathy Rolfson, Dave DeRoche, Sherry Jacobs, Peter Munoz, Lois Price, Marj Blackwell, Jill Day, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Irene Thompson, Ron Day, Joanne Larson, Bonnie Sherwood, Jim Kellogg, Melba Yee, Sandra Cook, Quincy Dong, Martin Levy, Bob Wong, Peggy Shultz, Denny McGee, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Judy Love, Lisa Euphrat, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Phil Witte, Joyce Ahern, Priscilla Wanerus, Bill Ahern, Leigh Sorensen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Stella Houston’s goddaughter Leilani Ching, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Melissa Clark, and Kim Blumberg who were walking with them for the first time. By Dick Carter Last Wednesday, October 30, the Walking on Wednesdays group had its annual pre-Halloween tour of Mountain View Cemetery. They are pictured in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum. Forty-six walkers with four K-9 best friends were on hand. The tour was conducted by longtime docent Jane Leroe. Jane has an extensive knowledge of the Mountain View Cemetery and loves sharing it. Jane’s women’s tour of the historic cemetery included some famous women who made significant contributions in law, medicine, education, and architecture. The suffragist movement which resulted in women gaining the right to vote in California in 1911 was also part of it. Jane took the group inside to the mausoleum’s chapel for her introductory remarks. Seeing it was a treat. It was serene with lots of marble. In the early 1860s a group of twelve leading businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and the 13th mayor of Oakland (1867 to 1869), decided the area needed a private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better. They bought 200 acres of fields far from the center of Oakland at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery was established in 1863. Twenty-six acres were added later. Approximately 170,000 people are buried at Mountain View, and there is room for an additional equal number. The founders’ contract with Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park and Stanford University, called for him to get $1,000. No women were involved in the cemetery’s development. Some made good use of their deceased husbands’ money when they took up permanent residence at Mountain View. There are also many self-made, successful women buried in the cemetery. Jane led the group through the back of the mausoleum and up a hill to the Colton tomb. David Colton was the business manager for the “Big 4,” the men who built the transcontinental railroad. These men should probably be called the “Big 4½.” After David’s death Ellen was involved in a lawsuit in which she showed the men’s correspondence telling how they bribed lawmakers. Then it was over to the grave of Clara Bedell, a well-known madame in San Francisco in the latter part of the 19th century. Her “house of ill-repute” was located on Post Street near Union Square in San Francisco. In 1891, at the age of 37, she was found dead in her room. It appeared she had mixed opium with some wine and overdosed. Three years after her death she was named the beneficiary of a $10,000 life insurance policy of a local judge. Jane noted many women with remarkable histories and accomplishments. Miranda Lux provided $500,000 for California schools. Chloe Buckel was orphaned at age four but became a doctor and an advocate for education. Mary McHenry Keith was the first woman to graduate from Hastings Law School. Ina Donna Coolbrith was California’s first poet laureate. German-born Emma Marwedel started the first free kindergarten on the West Coast. Sara Lemmon is responsible for the California Poppy being named the State flower. Mary Williams was the New York World’s only women cartoonist and advocated for women’s suffrage in her work. Kate Kirkham provided free medical services for the poor and created a Fabiola Society Hospital that was bought by Kaiser. Anna Head started the K-12 school in 1887 that still bears her name today. Architect Julia Morgan, likely the most famous woman buried at Mountain View, is in a family plot. She is listed sixth on a plaque with other family members because she wanted to be buried with them, and let her monuments reflect her accomplishments. Jane told these stories and more in a fact-filled, highly enjoyable tour on a lovely day. At the morning’s end the walkers expressed thanks to Jane for a most enjoyable pre-Halloween tour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. I have spent the last 23 years that I have been writing this column tasting in Napa, Sonoma, Medocino, the Santa Cruz Mountains, the Santa Lucia Highlands and Livermore. All these areas are an embarrassment of riches. Still, it was nice on a recent journey to Southern California to visit family that I had the occasion to visit some tasting rooms in Santa Barbara. I was somewhat familiar with the southern California wine scene as I had spent my college years at Pepperdine University in Malibu and spent many weekends exploring the wineries of the Santa Ynez Valley and Santa Barbara. Since those early days, Santa Barbara has become an amazing location for wine tasting. The city is literally stuffed with wine tasting rooms; in fact they have an entire area called “The Funk Zone” that is dedicated to wine tasting rooms, trendy restaurants and wine bars. Time was short this visit so I concentrated on two wineries – one an old standby and one that was new to me. manager who walked us through many of the winery’s offerings. The house style of the Au Bon Climat wines is finesse rather than drama. Clenendon’s passion for the wines of Burgundy shines through as the wines are refined are structured without excessive fruit or sugar. • 2023 Au Bon Climat Pinot Gris/Pinot Blanc $22 Beautiful grapefruit and lemon aromas jump out of the glass followed by aromas of pears and apples. The wine is round and juicy as well as savory on the pretty potent palate, and it reveals stimulating saline acidity. It is the perfect aperitif wine. • 2021 Au Bon Climat Chardonnay “Foresight” $40 Hailing from the historic Bien Nacido Vineyard and some of the oldest vines in Santa Barbara County, this wine displays a sun-kissed nose of apricot and peaches and a medley of oak-derived baking spices. On the palate it matches this power with a soft, glossy texture and a generous finish of ripe fruits with additional touches of vanilla. The Talley Pinot Noir was Pierre’s favorite. • 2022 Au Bon Climat Pinot Noir Talley Vineyard “Rosemary’ $75 Au Bon Climat makes a ton of different Pinot Noirs and all were above average in quality but this one was my favorite. Aged in 100% new oak, the perfumed, vanilla nose was redolent of violets and roses. Vibrant notes of cherries and currants strut from the glass leading to a silky, direct palate and a refreshing and taut finish. This is a Burgundian styled wine with California-sized fruit. • 2028 Clenenden Family Nebbiolo “Punta Exclamitiva” $75 My daughter Shelby said this wine smelled like an old church. She nailed it – imagine slate floors, dust, and faded floral bouquets. Add to that lavender, cherries, crème de cassis and dried herbs. It is tremendously layered and complex and changes dramatically in the glass as it airs. Nebbiolo is famously hard to grow anywhere except its native Piedmonte which makes this wine even more impressive. The finest New World Nebbiolo I have tasted.
